steps.observation: (d) fine uniform features ~0.3-0.8 um, far finer than (b),(c) at the same 2 um scale  +  IPF maps: (a) equiaxed grains mostly ~0.5-1.5 um; (c) equiaxed grains ~1.5-3 um
steps.key: The EBSD IPF maps establish that the equiaxed features visible in panels (a) and (c) are genuine crystallographic grains, sized about 0.5-1.5 um in (a) and about 1.5-3 um in (c). The SEM image separately shows that panel (d) contains much finer, uniform equiaxed features (about 0.3-0.8 um) than panels (b) and (c) imaged at the same 2 um scale. Put together, the pair supports reading the finer SEM features in (d) as a continuation of the same equiaxed-grain trend down to a smaller size -- i.e., the grain/feature size decreases from the EBSD-confirmed ~1.5-3 um grains in (c) toward the ~0.3-0.8 um features seen by SEM in (d).

steps.observation: XRD reflections indexed to L12 (incl. weak superlattice peaks near 25 and 35 deg) and B2 (near 31, 44.6 deg)  +  At first strain step one lamella is featureless while the neighbour shows mottled contrast and line contrast along the interface
steps.key: The as-cast alloy is confirmed (by XRD) to contain two ordered phases (L12 and B2), and at the first strain step the TEM pair shows one lamella remaining featureless while its neighbor develops mottled contrast plus line contrast along the interface -- together indicating that the two-phase system responds asymmetrically to strain, with one lamella type acquiring visible internal contrast and the other not.

steps.observation: Dense dislocation band labelled as pile-up along a lamella boundary
steps.key: Read together, the earlier TEM contrast asymmetry (one lamella featureless, its neighbor developing mottled contrast plus line contrast along the interface) and the dense dislocation pile-up band at a lamella boundary (F4a, F4c) support that the mottled/line contrast seen in the responding lamella corresponds to a dislocation-based mechanism -- specifically pile-up of dislocations at the lamella boundary -- rather than to a non-defect (e.g., purely diffraction or strain-field) contrast effect. The combination thus upgrades the earlier qualitative 'asymmetric contrast' observation to an asymmetric defect (dislocation pile-up) response localized at the interface of one lamella type.

steps.observation: Many straight parallel dislocation lines on one slip trace across the field
steps.key: Read together, the pile-up band at the lamella boundary (Observation A) and the field of many straight, parallel dislocation lines along a single slip trace (Observation B, F5b) show that the microstructure contains at least two qualitatively distinct dislocation morphologies -- a tangled/pile-up arrangement localized at an interface and a separate, orderly parallel-line arrangement along a slip trace elsewhere in the field. This supports that dislocation behavior differs by location/phase in this material (i.e., the two lamella types are not responding to strain in the same way), beyond what either observation shows alone.

steps.observation: TEM bright-field: parallel alternating straight lamellae A and B with sharp interfaces  +  At first strain step one lamella is featureless while the neighbour shows mottled contrast and line contrast along the interface
steps.key: Taken together, the baseline two-phase lamellar architecture with sharp A/B interfaces (Observation A) and the asymmetric contrast that appears at the first strain step (Observation B) support that the alternating lamellar structure is the substrate on which strain is partitioned unequally between the two lamella types: one lamella type stays featureless while its neighbour develops mottled contrast and line contrast along the interface, i.e. the onset of plastic deformation is phase-selective and interface-localized rather than uniform across the microstructure.

steps.observation: Dense dislocation band labelled as pile-up along a lamella boundary
steps.key: Read together with the earlier phase-selective, interface-localized onset of plasticity (mottled contrast and line contrast along one lamella's interface, versus a featureless neighbour), the dense dislocation band identified as a pile-up along a lamella boundary gives a concrete microstructural reading of that interface-localized contrast: the line contrast at the boundary noted in the earlier result is consistent with dislocation pile-up accumulating against the phase boundary, rather than being an artifact or a diffuse feature spread through the lamella. The pair together therefore supports that the interface itself, not just one of the two phases in isolation, is a site where dislocations are accumulating at this strain step, and that the earlier-noted asymmetry has a boundary-localized dislocation signature.

steps.observation: Inset true stress rises from ~410 to ~1070 MPa up to 0.06 true strain
steps.key: Taken together, the interface-localized dislocation pile-up seen at the first strain step (A) and the macroscopic stress-strain response (B, true stress rising from ~410 to ~1070 MPa up to 0.06 true strain) support that the microstructural dislocation accumulation at the lamella boundary is occurring in a material that is simultaneously undergoing substantial macroscopic strain hardening, i.e. the boundary-localized pile-up process and the bulk hardening behavior co-occur in the same deforming microstructure rather than being unrelated observations from different experiments.
